title: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי

paragraphs: (1) In the Mishnah: Avot 2:8; Shabbat 16:7, 22:3; Shekalim 1:4; Sukkah 2:5, 3:12; Rosh Hashanah 4:1, 3, 4; Ketubbot 13:1, 2; Sotah 5:2, 5, 9:9, 15. As ‘Ben Zakkai’: Sanhedrin 5:2; Eduyot 8:3, 7; Menachot 10:5; Kelim 2:2, 17:16; Yadayim 4:3, 6.

(2) The priest: so writes Maimonides in his introduction to Zeraim. Indeed, Rashi, Shabbat 34a, writes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was a priest, as we say in tractate Parah—chapter 1, so in the new Talmud edition. But I did not find it there, only in the Tosefta, Parah, chapter 3, and Oholot, chapter 16. His students asked Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: ‘In what garments is the cow prepared?’ He replied: ‘In gold garments.’ They told him: ‘You taught us, in white garments.’ He replied: ‘You have spoken well. If I forgot a deed my hands performed and my eyes saw, how much more something my ears heard!’ It was not that he did not know, but that he sought to spur the students on. Some say that they asked Hillel the Elder; it was not that he did not know, but, and so forth. In Sifrei, beginning of Chukkat: ‘If I forgot what my hands performed.’ Yet Tosafot, Menachot 21b, write: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai said, ‘But the priests expound this verse for themselves.’ This implies that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was not a priest. The baraita in Sifrei, ‘What my hands served,’ and so forth, means not that he personally did it, but that it was done according to his instruction. As for Sifrei’s ‘Some say it was Hillel, but he could not say “what my hands performed and served”’—meaning, perhaps this too was done according to his instruction—the reason is that no cow was burned in his days. End quotation. Piskei Tosafot there, section 21, likewise writes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was not a priest. Rashi’s view also requires examination: if Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai prepared a cow, and ‘the work of my hands’ is understood literally, why does Parah 3:5, which lists those who burned cows, not count him?

(3) He received from Hillel and Shammai (Avot, chapter 2). Yuchasin, in the sequence of transmission from Yesod Olam, says: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rabbi Shimon ben Hillel received from Hillel and Shammai. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s colleagues were Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov—see his entry; this is false—and Rabbi Tzadok and his son Rabbi Elazar—this too is incorrect; see his entry—and Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha the high priest; Abba Shaul of Beit Ramsha, see his entry; Rabbi Elazar of Modiin, see his entry; Rabbi Chanina the deputy high priest, see his entry; Rabban Gamliel the Elder and his son Rabbi Shimon, who was killed; Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos—this requires examination—and Rabbi Chananyah ben Teradyon—this requires examination—and Shmuel HaKatan; Rabbi Eliezer ben Perata; Rabbi Elazar ben Dama—see his entry, this is incorrect; Rabbi Yehudah ben Bava—this requires examination; Chananyah ben Chakhinai—see his entry, this is incorrect; and Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa—this is incorrect, see his entry, for he went to study with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and therefore was not his colleague. Shalshelet HaKabbalah 33a writes: ‘I saw in Ellu Terefot: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai said, “I remember when I sat seventeen rows behind Rav before Rabbi.”’ He erred, for this was said by Rabbi Yochanan, not ben Zakkai, as in Chullin 137b; see above, Abba Arikha. Something similar is in Chullin 54a. ‘Maharik, section 169, writes that there were two men named Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, or that this was a different Rabbenu HaKadosh.’ End of Shalshelet HaKabbalah’s quotation. Certainly he encountered an erroneous text. Maharik’s responsa are not before me now; perhaps Maharik too should read ‘Rabbi Yochanan,’ meaning the unqualified Rabbi Yochanan, not ben Zakkai. Thus there was one Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and no second.

(4) He was born in 3713 and lived 120 years: forty years he engaged in commerce, forty years he served the sages, and forty years he led. Rosh Hashanah 31b; Sanhedrin 41a; Bereshit Rabbah, end of Vayechi; and the end of Sifrei. Sanhedrin 41b relates: when he was learning they called him Ben Zakkai—an incident in which Ben Zakkai examined the witnesses about fig stalks. When he taught, they called him Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. When the account calls him Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, it uses his present designation. His court was in Beror Chayil before the destruction: Sanhedrin 32b. Rabbi Yehoshua went to him at Beror Chayil: Tosefta, Maaserot, chapter 2. Thus we find laws established before the forty years during which he led Israel, in Rosh Hashanah and Sukkah. It appears from Rosh Hashanah that most of his forty years of leadership were while the Temple stood. Accordingly, in the time of Rabban Gamliel the Elder and his son Rabbi Shimon, who was killed at the destruction, he too led, or was head of the court, since others were Nesiim. At least he was Nasi for two years after the destruction, as Rashi writes at the end of Rosh Hashanah, 31b, end: ‘A year or two.’ Shalshelet HaKabbalah, page 27, says Titus made Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai Nasi, and he presided for three years after the destruction, as appears in HaNizakin and Avot de-Rabbi Natan. Yuchasin 22a says that he was Nasi for five years—a scribal error. He instituted nine enactments after the destruction, in the Mishnah, Sukkah 41a. Tosafot, Bammeh Behemah, 54b, say Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai presided for two years after the destruction, before Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh presided; see there for why Rabban Gamliel was not Nasi after his father Rabbi Shimon’s killing. He died in 3833, five years after the destruction; so writes Tzemach David. Accordingly, one may say that in his lifetime, after being Nasi for two or three years, he gave the presidency to Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh. See below, under Rabbi Yishmael the high priest, what I wrote in Sefer Keritot’s name: after the destruction Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai maintained an academy in Yavneh for forty years. This opposes Rashi and Tosafot. During his presidency he was in Yavneh, as Rashi writes in Rosh Hashanah 31b, beginning: when the Sanhedrin went into exile from Jerusalem to Yavneh in Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s days; see Rabban Gamliel the Elder. Although he went to Dimsit, as related in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 14: when his son died, his students came to console him. He accepted no consolation until Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah entered—another reading, Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh—and he accepted consolation. When he went out from before him he said: ‘I shall go to Dimsit, a beautiful place with beautiful water.’ They said: ‘We shall go to Yavneh, a place with many Torah scholars.’ The one who went to Dimsit declined in his Torah reputation; those who went to Yavneh grew in reputation. This was before his presidency. In Midrash Kohelet, on ‘For oppression makes a wise man foolish,’ and so forth: as long as he lived, his five students were before him. When he died they went to Yavneh, while Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh went to Emmaus; see his entry. Shabbat 147b says Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh went to Dimsit, and so forth, and forgot his learning. Yoma 39b: forty years before the destruction the Sanctuary’s gates opened, until Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuked them. In Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 4, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai told the people of Jerusalem to make peace with Vespasian. They did not listen. He told his students Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua to make him a coffin, and they took him out as though he were dead. He came before Vespasian and found favor with him. After Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was killed, he asked the emperor to save his son Rabban Gamliel, and for a physician for Rabbi Tzadok; see his entry. See HaNizakin and Midrash Eichah. Although he was very old, he was head of the Sanhedrin, even though one does not seat an old man, a eunuch, or a man without children on the Sanhedrin, as related in the chapter Echad Dinei Mamonot. For the reason, see Nachalat Binyamin and Beer Sheva.

(5) He was called ‘the peddlers’ basket’; when he died, the splendor of wisdom ceased: the chapter Eglah Arufah, 49. In the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chapter 2, mishnah 3, his tefillin did not move from him, in summer or winter; likewise his student Rabbi Eliezer. No person ever greeted him first, even a gentile in the marketplace: Berakhot 17a. In Bereshit Rabbah, section 15, he said that if all the seas were ink and the heavens sheets, they would not suffice to write what he had learned from his teachers; he had diminished it no more than a dog lapping from the sea. Sukkah 28 and Bava Batra 134: he did not engage in idle conversation. ‘An incident came before him in Arav’: Rashi, Shabbat 121a, end, explains it as a place, and there, 146a, Rashi explains it as a region. In Rosh Hashanah 18a, there was a family in Jerusalem whose members died at eighteen. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai told them: ‘Perhaps you belong to Eli’s family; occupy yourselves with Torah.’ They did so and lived. In tractate Derekh Eretz, chapter 6, he sent Rabbi Yehoshua to Shimon ben Antipatros—see his entry—who used to flog anyone who ate with him. In Tosefta, Maaserot, chapter 5, and in Bammeh Madlikin and Osin Passin, 19a, ‘in Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s school’: Rashi explains this as a baraita arranged in his study house, like Rabbi Chiyya’s Tosefta; see his entry. He instituted enactments: Rosh Hashanah 29, 30, 31.

(6) He saw four Nesiim: Hillel, from whom he received; his son Rabbi Shimon; Rabban Gamliel the Elder; and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who was killed. In Hillel’s and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s days there were two high priests, Chanamel the Egyptian and Yishmael ben Pabi. Yochanan the high priest was in his days; see his entry. This requires examination. He had a son, a great sage called Rabbi Yehudah, who disputes with Rabbi Akiva in Kol HaYad. Perhaps he is Rabbi Yehudah HaKohen; see his entry. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Yishmael—perhaps Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha the high priest, since the Rabbi Yishmael who disputes with Rabbi Akiva was a student of Rabbi Yehoshua, his student; or Rabbi Yishmael ben Chananyah mentioned below in Avot de-Rabbi Natan—Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh, Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, and Rabbi Akiva were sitting and expounding the moon’s birth: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 7. This requires examination, because Rabbi Akiva too was a student of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer. Avot, chapter 2, says he had five students: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah, Rabbi Yose HaKohen, Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel—in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 14, the reading is ‘and Yishmael ben Chananyah’—and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh. In Beitzah 5b, Rabbi Eliezer’s students told Rabbi Eliezer: ‘Your colleagues have already voted on your case’; this means Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, although he was his teacher; see his entry. When he became ill and near death, his students came to visit him. He began weeping. They said: ‘Our master, lamp of Israel, right-hand pillar, mighty hammer, why do you weep?’ He replied: ‘Were they leading me before flesh and blood,’ and so forth. At his departure he said: ‘Remove the vessels because of the impurity, and prepare a chair for Hezekiah king of Judah, who is coming’: Berakhot 28b; Jerusalem Talmud, Avodah Zarah 3:1 and end of Sotah. See Berit Shalom, Metzora, for why he commanded two things. Gilgulei Neshamot (cited as ג״נ), letter peh, writes that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, and Rabbi are one spark. Chesed LeAvraham, spring 5, stream 25, says Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rabbi Akiva are the mystery of Moses’ two arms mingled in Cain; hence their years are equal. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was Jacob; see above, Rabbi Akiva. At Tiberias, before the town, Maimonides is buried; beside it, at the study house, Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Kahana were buried; beside it, in the cemetery, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his students were buried (גא״י; provisionally Gelilot Eretz Yisrael). In Benjamin’s Travels: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rabbi Yonatan ben Levi.

(7) He spoke to Ben Bukhri. He spoke to the Bene Beteira. Rabbi Berekhiah transmitted in his name. He said: ‘Chanan ben Avshalom spoke well.’ Rabbi Yehoshua bar Nechemyah transmitted in his name. Rabbi Nechunyah ben HaKanah was his student; this requires examination. In Chullin 27, ‘They further asked’: Rashi explains that Kontreikon asked Rabban Gamliel; Tosafot write that he asked Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. Rabbah bar Mari transmitted in his name.
